DEVORE-01-NTLM-LMCOMPATIBILITYLEVEL Require NTLMv2 (LAN Manager authentication level)

HIGHFailstage: not startedCONFLICTCan lock people out

NTLMv1 and LM responses can be cracked or relayed quickly, so anyone who captures one can sign in as that user.

Microsoft changes this default: October 2026. Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025 switch BlockNtlmv1SSO to enforce by default, blocking NTLMv1 credentials for signed-in users (unless Credential Guard is on). Microsoft

Found: 1 in Sample Workstation Baseline GPO; 5 in Sample Override GPOTarget: at least 5 (step 1: at least 3)

Conflict — enforced-override

2 GPOs set this key to different values, linked to different parts of the domain: Sample Workstation Baseline GPO = 1 on DC=test,DC=local; Sample Override GPO = 5 on OU=Domain Controllers,DC=test,DC=local (enforced). The enforced value wins only under its own link; machines elsewhere get the other value. Check with gpresult on a machine from each part.

Precedence is unresolved. Confirm the effective value with gpresult /h or the Group Policy Results (RSoP) wizard on a representative machine before changing or trusting any of these settings.

Next: step 1: set it to 3.

Before enforcing, check: Look for event 4624 with LmPackageName = 'NTLM V1' on member servers and endpoints, ignoring ANONYMOUS LOGON. Event 4776 on DCs doesn't record the NTLM version, so it can't be used for this.

  • IN STAGES: don't set domain controllers to 5 until every device is at 3 or higher. At 5, a DC treats NTLMv1 attempts as bad passwords, which locks accounts out (Devore saw 46 failed logons from one NTLMv1 SMB connection).
  • TATTOOING: the value lives outside HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies, so if you later set the policy back to 'Not Defined', the old value stays on each device and has to be cleared there.
How to fix it, step by step
Remediation

Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level'. Set every client and member server to 'Send NTLMv2 response only' (3) first. Only then raise domain controllers to 'Refuse LM & NTLM' (5).

How to roll it out safely

Step 1: set it to 3 first. Machines send only NTLMv2. This already changes behaviour: a device or server that only accepts LM or NTLMv1, such as an old NAS or copier, stops working with them. Domain controllers still accept anything until step 2.

Step 2: only then set it to 5. Don't skip step 1: enforcing before every device and service account is ready can cause sign-in failures and account lockouts.

More notes (2)
  • Levels 0-3 control what a client sends; levels 4-5 control what a server or DC accepts.
  • Credential Guard disables NTLMv1 by itself and ignores this setting. No reboot is required.

DEVORE-05-LDAP-CHANNEL-BINDING Domain controller LDAP channel binding

HIGHFailstage: not startedno GPO sets thisCan lock people out

Channel binding stops an attacker relaying someone's LDAPS sign-in to a domain controller.

Found: no GPO sets thisTarget: exactly 2 (step 1: exactly 1)

Next: step 1: set it to 1.

Before enforcing, check: Event 3075 (2019+) or 3039 (2016 and earlier) in the Directory Service log.

  • AUDIT FIRST: Server 2019 and later log event 3075; Server 2016 and earlier only log 3039, when a bind is rejected. Both need '16 LDAP Interface Events' at 2 or higher.
How to fix it, step by step
Remediation

Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Domain controller: LDAP server channel binding token requirements' = 'When supported' (1) while you audit, then 'Always' (2).

How to roll it out safely

Step 1: set it to 1 first. Domain controllers check the channel binding token from every client that sends one, and still accept clients that send none. That already rejects clients whose token doesn't match, which is common behind load balancers that terminate TLS, so test first.

Step 2: only then set it to 2. Don't skip step 1: enforcing before every device and service account is ready can cause sign-in failures and account lockouts.

More notes (2)
  • Devore gives the setting names (Never / When supported / Always) but not the numbers. The 0/1/2 mapping is the widely used one from KB4034879; confirm it against a baseline source.
  • Unset means off. It only affects SASL binds over TLS. Load balancers that terminate or bridge TLS break channel binding, and a load-balanced name (VIP FQDN) must be in the DC certificate's SAN.

DEVORE-06-SMB-CLIENT-SIGNING-ALWAYS SMB client always requires signing

HIGHFailstage: not startedno GPO sets thisPilot first

Without SMB signing, an attacker can relay a captured sign-in to a file server and act as that user.

Found: no GPO sets thisTarget: exactly 1

Next: set it to 1.

How to fix it, step by step
Remediation

Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)' = Enabled, on endpoints and member servers as well as domain controllers.

How to roll it out safely

Set it to 1. This can break some devices or apps. Link it to a small pilot OU first, and widen it once nothing breaks.

More notes (3)
  • NOT THE LEGACY SETTING: this isn't 'Digitally sign communications (if server agrees)' (EnableSecuritySignature). That's a different, weaker setting that only affects SMBv1: Microsoft says SMB2 and later ignore it, and recommends against it. A GPO setting EnableSecuritySignature = 1 doesn't satisfy this check, which doesn't read that value.
  • '(always)' applies to every SMB version and drops the session when the other side can't sign.
  • Windows 11 24H2 and Server 2025 require SMB signing by default, so on those an unset value doesn't necessarily mean unsigned traffic. It's still not enforced by policy, which is what this check looks for.

Where the value comes fromMicrosoft, 'Overview of Server Message Block signing in Windows', for 'Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)': registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanManWorkstation\Parameters, value RequireSecuritySignature, REG_DWORD, 0 (disable) or 1 (enable): https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/storage/file-server/smb-signing-overview. That 'always' means signing is required is from Microsoft, 'Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)': https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/microsoft-network-client-digitally-sign-communications-always. The key is written as Microsoft writes it ('LanMan', capital M). Real GPOs spell the service name several ways, and ADitor matches it regardless of case.
Found (this scan)

Scan notes
  • No GPO requires SMB signing on the client side, so outbound SMB is signed only when the server requires it. ADitor doesn't assume a Windows default here: the policy's documented default is Disabled, but Windows 11 24H2 and Server 2025 require signing by default, so what an unset value means depends on the Windows version, which a GPO scan can't see.

DEVORE-07-UNCONSTRAINED-DELEGATION No accounts other than domain controllers have unconstrained delegation

HIGHFailstage: not startedread from the directoryPilot first

A computer with unconstrained delegation keeps the tickets of everyone who connects to it, admins included, so taking it over can mean taking over the domain.

Found: 1 listed: APPSRV01$Target: none

Next: fix the 1 listed on the card.

How to fix it, step by step
Remediation

For each listed account, switch to constrained delegation or resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD) for only the services it needs, then turn off 'Trust this computer/user for delegation to any service'.

How to roll it out safely
More notes (3)
  • Changing delegation can break the services that depend on it. Find out what each listed account delegates to before changing it, and change one at a time.
  • Only writable domain controllers are excluded. Read-only domain controllers don't carry this flag by design, so one that has it is listed, as is any user account, whatever its primary group.
  • Disabled accounts are listed and marked: re-enabling one brings the exposure back.

Where the rule comes fromDevore Part 7: accounts trusted for delegation to any service (userAccountControl TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION, 0x80000) should be moved to constrained or resource-based constrained delegation. Writable domain controllers carry this flag by design and are excluded, recognised by their account type (a computer account with SERVER_TRUST_ACCOUNT, 0x2000), not by primary group.

DEVORE-08-NTLM-AUDIT-INCOMING Audit incoming NTLM traffic

MEDIUMFailstage: not startedno GPO sets thisSafe: logging only

Shows which clients still use NTLM against this system, which you need to know before restricting it.

Found: no GPO sets thisTarget: at least 1

Next: set it to 1.

How to fix it, step by step
Remediation

Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > 'Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit Incoming NTLM Traffic' = 'Enable auditing for domain accounts' (or 'for all accounts').

How to roll it out safely

Set it to 1. This only turns on logging, so it's safe to apply everywhere at once.

More notes (5)
  • MINIMUM, NOT EXACT LEVEL: 1 or higher means some auditing is on, and 0 fails as auditing turned off. Microsoft lists the options but not their numbers, so whether it audits domain accounts or all accounts is shown in the evidence, not judged. Read the value found if you need to know.
  • INFERRED, NOT CITED: Microsoft doesn't publish that 'Disable' is stored as 0 and the other options as 1 or higher. ADitor infers it from Microsoft's statement that the unset policy behaves as 'Disable'. 'Where the value comes from' explains why checking only a minimum is safe on that basis; the exact level is never judged.
  • WATCH OUT: some third-party write-ups mix up the Audit* and Restrict* values and say 2 here means 'deny all'. It doesn't. Microsoft says this audit policy doesn't block any traffic. Blocking is DEVORE-08-NTLM-BLOCK-INCOMING, which isn't checked yet because no source gives its value.
  • Rollout state 'enforced' here means the audit policy is fully set up, not that NTLM is blocked. Blocking is covered by the DEVORE-08-NTLM-BLOCK-* checks.
  • Logs events 8002 and 8003 in Microsoft/Windows/NTLM/Operational.

DEVORE-04-KDC-DEFAULTDOMAINSUPPORTEDENCTYPES Disable RC4 at the domain level on domain controllers

HIGHUnknownnot confirmed by this scanCan lock people out

While domain controllers still issue RC4 tickets, any account with an SPN is easier to crack offline (Kerberoasting).

  • Reported as 'unknown', not as a failure. This control's documented remediation is a direct registry write on the domain controllers, which leaves no trace in Group Policy at all, so the key appearing in no GPO is NOT evidence that the value is unset. This scan reads Group Policy and not the machines, so it cannot see the live value either way and issues no verdict. Check it on each domain controller with: reg query "HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\services\KDC" /v "DefaultDomainSupportedEncTypes"

How to fix it, step by step
Remediation

On domain controllers, set DefaultDomainSupportedEncTypes to 0x38. Do it last, after each service account has AES. Devore creates the value directly on the DCs; a GPO registry preference with the same value works the same way, and it's the only form this scan can see.

How to roll it out safely

Set it to 56. This can lock people out. Apply it to a pilot group first and read the warnings below.

More notes (2)

Where no GPO sets it, the result is 'unknown', not 'fail', and the finding includes the reg query command to check it on the DCs. Where a GPO does set it, for example as a registry preference, it's checked normally.

How to fix it, step by step
Remediation

On domain controllers, set the '16 LDAP Interface Events' diagnostic level to 2 or higher while you collect unsigned-bind evidence. Devore does this with a registry write on each DC: reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NTDS\Diagnostics" /v "16 LDAP Interface Events" /t REG_DWORD /d 2 /f. A GPO registry preference with the same value works the same way, and it's the only form this scan can see.

How to roll it out safely

Set it to 2. This only turns on logging, so it's safe to apply everywhere at once.

More notes (4)
  • NOT SET THROUGH GROUP POLICY: the documented fix writes the registry directly on each domain controller, so this scan can't confirm the level. Where no GPO sets it, the result is 'unknown', not 'fail', and the finding includes the reg query command to check it on the DCs.
  • This turns on logging; it doesn't harden anything by itself. It produces events 2889 (client IP, account, bind type), 2887 (daily unsigned count) and 2888 (binds rejected once signing is required).
  • Left on permanently it's noisy, so it's usually raised only for the audit period.
  • Levels run 0-5, more verbose as they rise (Microsoft, 'AD and LDS diagnostic event logging'; default 0). A level above 2 logs more, including the 2889 events, so it passes. The minimum is 2; it doesn't have to be exactly 2.

DEVORE-04-SPN-ACCOUNTS-AES Service accounts with an SPN state AES in msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes stage: enforced found none
Expected (baseline)
Expectednothing found by the directory query
Where the rule comes fromDevore Part 4: service accounts with an SPN should carry the AES bits in msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes. AES bits per Microsoft: 0x8 (AES128) and 0x10 (AES256). A blank value makes the account use the domain default, which depends on patch level: before the 2026 Kerberos updates the domain controllers assume 0x27 (RC4 tickets); from April 2026 (enforcement enabled) and July 2026 (automatic) they assume AES only (0x18), per Microsoft's CVE-2026-20833 guidance: https://support.microsoft.com/en-gb/topic/how-to-manage-kerberos-kdc-usage-of-rc4-for-service-account-ticket-issuance-changes-related-to-cve-2026-20833-1ebcda33-720a-4da8-93c1-b0496e1910dc. An account that explicitly lists RC4 without AES keeps getting RC4 tickets after those updates.

How ADitor decides

This scan doesn't work out which GPO wins when several set the same setting (policy precedence, RSoP). It reports every GPO that sets it, with its link path, and flags disagreements as conflicts. For a conflict, check the effective value with gpresult /h before acting.

Every target value comes from a cited source, shown on each card under Where the value comes from. Where no source gives a value, the setting is listed under Not covered yet rather than guessed.

These notes apply to several checks, so they are listed here once rather than on each card:

  • A pass means nothing the bind account can read matched. AD silently leaves out objects and attributes an account isn't allowed to read, so run the scan with an account that can read the whole domain (an ordinary domain user can by default); a domain whose permissions were tightened can hide findings from a weaker account.

Catalog notes
  • Check types in this release: gpo-security-template (GptTmpl.inf [Registry Values]), gpo-registry-pol (Registry.pol and Preferences Registry.xml) and directory-state. A directory-state control names a fixed, read-only directory query in directory_check and asserts that it finds nothing: none is a pass, any is a fail listing them, and a query that fails is an error. The spec's other directory-state controls (DEVORE-02 SMBv1, which the directory cannot show; DEVORE-08 Protected Users; the rest of DEVORE-07) are not in the catalog yet.
  • registry_key is the full path including the value name (its last component). For gpo-registry-pol the evaluator splits the last component off to match Registry.pol's separate key/value fields; for gpo-security-template the whole path is one [Registry Values] key.
  • Rollout is phased, not binary: interim_expected is the audit/negotiate step and final_expected the enforced step, so a domain correctly mid-rollout reports rollout_state 'audit' and result 'pass', not a failure.
  • os_default records the value Windows uses when no GPO sets the key, and only where a Microsoft document states it. Such a finding is evaluated against the default and marked 'source: os-default', so an assumed value is never mistaken for an enforced one. It is deliberately absent where there is no default to cite — LdapEnforceChannelBinding, for one, has no such key by default (channel binding is off), which is precisely why configuring it matters. Two limitations are deliberate. A finding resting on a default is capped at rollout_state 'audit', because 'enforced' means Group Policy holds the value and nothing enforces a default. And os_default is a single value, so a default that depends on the machine's role cannot be expressed: DEVORE-06-SMB-SERVER-SIGNING-ALWAYS is 'Enabled' by Microsoft's table for domain controllers but 'Disabled' for member servers and clients. Making that expressible would need the evaluator to know which machines a GPO lands on, which a SYSVOL/GPO scan cannot see at all — so those controls carry no default and say why in missing_note, rather than asserting one role's default over the whole domain.
